alignment.note: The Peshitta ܘܐܡܝܢ prefixes the conjunction waw ('and/now amen'), absorbing the function of Greek δέ into the opening particle; Greek and Latin keep ἀμήν / Amen as a bare interjection. This reflects standard Syriac discourse style of clause-initial waw.
The Greek postpositive δέ ('now/but') has no discrete equivalent in either the Vulgate (asyndetic Amen dico) or the Peshitta, which has instead absorbed the connective into the prefixed waw on ܘܐܡܝܢ.

Greek λέγω is a synthetic first-person present; the Peshitta renders it analytically with participle plus enclitic pronoun ܐܡܪ ܐܢܐ ('saying [am] I'), the normal Syriac means of expressing the present, whereas Latin dico matches the Greek synthetic form.

Greek pairs ὅπου with the conditional particle ἐάν ('wherever'); Latin compresses this into the single indefinite relative adverb Ubicumque, while the Peshitta uses ܕܟܠ ܐܝܟܐ ('that everywhere/wheresoever'), an idiomatic Syriac universalising construction with prefixed d-.

Greek κηρυχθῇ is a single aorist passive subjunctive; the Latin renders the future-perfect periphrasis prædicatum fuerit ('shall have been preached'), and the Peshitta ܕܬܬܟܪܙ keeps a single inflected verb with the subordinating d-, all conveying the same conditional-future sense.
εἰς ὅλον τὸν κόσμον / ܒܟܠܗ ܥܠܡܐ / in universo mundo.

Greek καί and Latin et are the simple connective 'and/also'; the Peshitta intensifies with ܘܐܦ ('and even/also'), a slightly emphatic adverbial pairing that heightens the contrast introduced in the apodosis.

Greek uses the neuter relative pronoun ὅ ('what'); the Vulgate matches with quod, while the Peshitta employs the indefinite noun ܡܕܡ ('the thing/somewhat') followed by the relative clause, a typical Syriac periphrasis for a relative substantive.

Greek and Latin express 'for a memorial of her' analytically with preposition plus noun plus genitive pronoun (εἰς μνημόσυνον αὐτῆς / in memoriam ejus); the Peshitta compresses the whole phrase into a single prefixed-and-suffixed form ܠܕܘܟܪܢܗ ('for-her-memorial'), characteristic of Syriac morphological synthesis.
